newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stadium beefs up security for Japan soccer.
newsitem.headline: HK stadium beefs up security for Japan soccer.

text.p: Hong Kong's stadium is drafting in extra security for a soccer match between a local side and a team from Japan because of a wave of anti-Japanese sentiment sweeping the territory.

Organisers of the soccer match said on Friday they were leaving nothing to chance. Police would boost their presence from a usual 30 or so to 175 and British soldiers would be employed as stewards for the October 22 game.
The British army confirmed off-duty troops can be hired as stewards for events in the stadium but they cannot be used to deal with trouble.
"They have permission to employ off-duty soldiers as stewards but if there's trouble they're not allowed to get involved," military spokesman Roger Goodwin told Reuters. "They have to withdraw."
Hong Kong has been awash with anti-Japanese protests over the past two months linked to a dispute over a group of islands claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan.

"Definitely they (British army soldiers) will be helping us man the stadium," spokeswoman Julia Lau of Wembley International (Hong Kong) said. The company manages the Hong Kong Stadium, located in the British colony's Happy Valley.
"The number (of soldiers) depends on the situation, the number of Japanese fans, Hong Kong spectators," Lau said.
Metal fences will skirt the pitch to protect players, and Japanese fans will be seated in a sectioned-off area of the stands. Organisers were also considering separate entrances.
The soldiers would trade fatigues for steward uniforms as part of a possibly 300-strong security team, which would be fielded instead of the usual 150 non-military security force.
The match between Japan's Grampus 8 and Hong Kong's South China side was postponed from Sunday October 20 to Tuesday October 22, but Lau could not give the reason for the switch.
Anti-Japanese sentiment has flared in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Macau since Japanese rightwing extremists built a lighthouse and planted flags on the rocky islets in the East China Sea in July.
Tokyo's claim to what it calls the Senkaku islands dates from 1895. China has also claimed the group as the Diaoyus for centuries.

Anger hit a new high last week when a Hong Kong activist drowned after jumping off a protest ship during a challenge to Japan's sovereignty claim over the islands. Tens of thousands of people turned out to mourn him in Hong Kong last Sunday.
On Friday, continuing their ritual daily ptotests, a small group of activists gathered outside a downtown Japanese department store and shouted for a boycott of Japanese goods.
